sections.h2: The Certificate of Continued Occupancy comes first
sections.html:
Before the title to a one or two family home can pass to a new owner, Fair Lawn wants a Certificate of Continued Occupancy. Price and closing date both hinge on how soon the Building Department inspects the house and signs off.

Fair Lawn is a Bergen County borough roughly 12 miles northwest of New York City. It had 34,927 residents in 2020 and an estimated 37,128 in 2025, up 6.3 percent. Only 5.14 square miles of land hold all those people, about 6,800 per square mile, so lots are tight and houses sit close together. Radburn, a planned community from 1929 and one of the first in the country, is inside the borough, and eight local sites are on the National Register of Historic Places. If your home is near one, ask the building office whether a review applies before you change the exterior.

Houses here are worth far more than the national figure, and few people move. These are 2020 to 2024 estimates.

The borough has 12,229 households averaging 2.90 people, and 78.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied. A sale near the median value falls in the $550,000 to $850,000 band of the state transfer fee schedule covered under closing costs.

sections.h2: What does the Certificate of Continued Occupancy involve?
sections.html:
The certificate is required for any transfer of title on a one or two family dwelling, and the borough's published fee is $175. The Building Department is in Room 112 of the municipal building, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is (201) 794-5307. Fire Prevention handles the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

  • You file an application and pay the $175 fee, then the department inspects the property and may photograph conditions.
  • The file also needs a smoke certificate from Fire Prevention, or a written waiver.
  • A failed public sidewalk must be repaired or replaced before the certificate is issued.
  • A buyer who flips the house has to apply again as the seller at the next sale.

If the buyer plans to do the repairs, the borough offers a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only, with no occupancy. The buyer's attorney sends a letter confirming the buyer understands that, and after closing the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175. On an as-is sale, the buyer must acknowledge that anything the inspection finds becomes the buyer's job to correct.

Most Fair Lawn addresses carry a hyphenated number, like the library's 10-01 Fair Lawn Avenue, and buyers searching online sometimes get no match unless they drop the dash. Nearly 10,000 addresses here use the system, almost half of all hyphenated addresses in New Jersey.

The first number gives the block distance from Broadway on north-south streets, or from the numbered street on east-west ones. Addresses south of Broadway or Route 4 begin with a zero. The system goes back to at least the 1930s and was built so emergency crews could find a house fast. Exceptions exist on the Glen Rock, Hawthorne and Saddle Brook sides and inside Radburn.

In your ad, write the address both with and without the dash, and check it against the tax record so title and survey work match the deed.

Two highways and two train stations make Fair Lawn a commuter town. Route 4 reaches the George Washington Bridge in under 10 miles from the Broadway district, and Route 208 runs northwest to Interstate 287. The Radburn and Broadway stations on NJ Transit's Bergen County Line serve Hoboken, with connections at Secaucus Junction to New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 144, 145, 148, 160, 164 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Local streets form a rough three-by-three grid. Saddle River Road, Plaza Road and River Road run north to south, while Broadway, Morlot Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue run east to west. Buyers also ask about the neighborhoods: Berdan Grove around Berdan Grove Park, the Broadway District shopping strip, and Radburn with its own station and pathways.

sections.h2: Closing steps and costs in Fair Lawn
sections.html:
The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the Bergen County Clerk records the deed. On a sale over $350,000 the rate climbs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 to $4.80 on the band from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 between $550,000 and $850,000. Above $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

New Jersey resident sellers, estates and trusts included, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. In an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so if one is rejected, resolve it with the clerk's office first and then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Assessment appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, which can give you the current filing deadline. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

Order matters in Fair Lawn because the certificate gates everything. Apply for it first, and ask Fire Prevention for the smoke certificate at the same time. Check the public sidewalk in front of the house, since a failed one holds up approval until it is fixed. Once the Building Department signs off, your closing attorney prepares the deed, the transfer fee and the GIT/REP form. Bring the deed, your latest tax bill and a payoff statement to that first meeting.

If a cash buyer wants to do the work, the Conditional Certificate lets title transfer without occupancy. That can shorten the wait for a seller, but the buyer must then apply for the full certificate after closing.

faqs.q: Does Fair Lawn require an inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. The borough requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title on a one or two family dwelling. The fee is $175, and applications go to Room 112 of the municipal building. Fire Prevention supplies the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take a Fair Lawn house that fails the inspection?
faqs.a: Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney sends a letter confirming there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk still has to be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

faqs.q: Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?
faqs.a: The executors who sign the deed sign it, or the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

faqs.q: Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?
faqs.a: The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms accept only the number without the dash.

faqs.q: Which county office records a Fair Lawn deed?
faqs.a: The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state transfer fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Your closing attorney or title company can confirm the filing method for your closing date.
